title: What’s the easiest language to learn?
summary: Duolingo teaching experts share what makes a language “easier” for some to learn, and how to choose what language you want to learn!
body_markdown:
Learning a language is tough, so it’s no wonder many of us have looked for shortcuts in the process! But whether a language is easy or[difficult](https://blog.duolingo.com/hardest-languages-to-learn/) depends on factors that are specific to each learner.


💡


No one language is objectively easier than the rest: Whether a language is easy or hard depends on your first language, your style of learning, and your motivation and exposure.


Let’s look at each of these factors in more detail:


- How similar the language is to your own
- Where the language’s complexities lie
- Your own goals with the language
- Your motivation and opportunities for learning


## A language similar to the one you know best is easier to learn


If you speak one of the over 100[language isolates](https://blog.duolingo.com/language-isolates/) without a close relative, this tip won’t be very useful. 🥲 But for English speakers, that means many languages from Europe (like Spanish and German) will be easier to learn on average than[languages that aren’t related](https://blog.duolingo.com/language-families-related-languages/) to English at all (like Arabic and Chinese), because Spanish and German are more similar to English.


But even this can be murky! For example, the English language is more[closely related to German](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-german-language/) than to French:[English is a Germanic language](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-english-language/) , while French is a[Romance language](https://blog.duolingo.com/what-are-romance-languages/) that evolved from Latin, like[Spanish](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-spanish/) and Italian. However, due to invasions and geographical proximity of modern-day France and England, many of the English words we use today were borrowed from French—so today, English shares a lot of its of vocabulary with French, even though grammatically, it has more in common with German!


We’re apt to[transfer](https://blog.duolingo.com/transfer-from-first-language/) elements from our first language to the new language—that can include vocabulary and grammar (like saying your new Spanish words[in the order you’d say them in English](https://blog.duolingo.com/how-to-make-sentences-in-spanish-french/) ). But we transfer other properties, too, like sounds (for spoken languages), handshapes and movements (for signed languages), and concepts and meanings (what counts as a *cup* versus a *glass* or *mug* ? where does[blue stop and green begin](https://blog.duolingo.com/color-words-around-the-world/) ?).


💡


Transfer can be helpful if the properties are the same across the languages, but can present a challenge if they differ.


Depending on[when and how you learned your languages](https://blog.duolingo.com/are-some-people-better-at-learning-languages/) , your brain might treat your *second* language as a sort of template for all other languages. If you’re learning a third or fourth language, you might actually be more likely to transfer properties of[your second language rather than your first](https://blog.duolingo.com/transfer-from-first-language/) !


## A language can have a mix of “easy” and “hard” properties


Because languages vary across so many properties (like sounds, meanings, sentence structure, and politeness), learning a new language[can be easy in some ways but difficult in others](https://blog.duolingo.com/language-irregularity-and-complexity/) .


For an English speaker, the sounds of Japanese might be (relatively) familiar, especially since it doesn’t have[tones](https://blog.duolingo.com/chinese-tones/) like Chinese or Vietnamese. But Japanese has[three writing systems](https://blog.duolingo.com/japanese-writing-systems/) and a very different[word order](https://blog.duolingo.com/how-to-make-sentences-in-spanish-french/) from English, which can make Japanese harder to learn in other ways. On the other hand, Chinese has a very challenging sound system for English speakers, but it **doesn’t** have verb tenses—and that might sound like a relief to any English speaker who is[learning Spanish](https://blog.duolingo.com/mistakes-in-spanish-for-learners/#5-spanish-verbs-conjugation) !


## “Learning” a language depends on your goals


“Learning” or “knowing” a language means different things to different learners: Do you want to get conversational for a trip to another country? Do you want to get a job that requires you to use the language professionally? Or do you want to[watch coverage of the Olympics](https://blog.duolingo.com/french-vocabulary-for-olympics/) *in* French?


Keep your own[personal goals](https://blog.duolingo.com/goldilocks-and-the-cefr-levels-which-proficiency-level-is-just-right/) in mind instead of being intimidated by a so-called “hard” language! Being a confident and effective communicator in a new language doesn’t necessarily mean having perfect grammar or[pronunciation](https://blog.duolingo.com/improve-pronunciation-in-new-language-tips/) . You can often make your way to conversational proficiency pretty quickly even with languages that have a reputation for being “hard.”


## Opportunity and motivation can make a language easier


How easy a language is to learn will also depend on how easy it is for you to get the tools you need to learn it. *Input* is language material you can learn from, whether that’s on an app, in a classroom, through conversations in a park, or from[watching movies in the language](https://blog.duolingo.com/language-practice-with-tv-movies/) . For example, if you’re an English speaker living in Seoul, it might be a lot easier for you to get good, high-quality Korean input than it is for you to get Spanish input, even though learning Spanish might be easier for you (on average).


Similarly,[motivation](https://blog.duolingo.com/how-to-keep-yourself-motivated-all-year-long/) is really important in language learning, since it takes a long time to build up high proficiency in a language. If you’re highly motivated to learn Norwegian because of family ties or because you want to attend grad school there, it’ll be easier for you to stick with it, compared to an otherwise “easier” language that you are less interested in sticking with for many months and years.


## Buckle up!


No matter which language you decide to study, the most important part of learning a new language is[sticking with it](https://blog.duolingo.com/sticking-with-it-tips-for-staying-motivated/) . Set practical, personal goals for your learning, and then make studying a regular habit that you can do a little at a time, for a long time. And check out[these tips](https://blog.duolingo.com/whats-the-best-way-to-learn-a-language/) for learning for the long haul!
